name: Submental dissection

lead: Submental dissection means working on the neck through an incision in the crease under the chin. Through it, a surgeon can remove or reposition fat, tighten or repair the platysma muscle and, when needed, address deeper structures. In looksmaxxing, it is discussed as part of the hardmaxx toolkit for creating a sharper jaw-to-neck line.

It is usually part of a neck lift or a combined procedure rather than a stand-alone cosmetic brand. Published surgical descriptions include platysmaplasty (bringing the muscle's edges together at the midline), and combinations with lateral suspension techniques.

paras: In surgery, an incision is placed under the chin, tissue is dissected to reach the area of concern, and the surgeon addresses fat, muscle bands or deeper fullness before closing, often alongside other neck or face-lift steps. Recovery details differ between surgeons and patients and are decided by the surgical team.

Reported risks of neck-lift surgery include bleeding or hematoma, infection, numbness, temporary nerve weakness, contour irregularities and recurrent platysmal bands. Over-removal of fat can lead to a hollowed 'cobra neck' look. Work on deeper structures can bring risks such as a saliva collection. Candidates should discuss risks with a board-certified surgeon.

chain: Incision in the crease under the chin
Fat, muscle bands or deeper fullness addressed
Sharper jaw-neck line and cervicomental angle
angle.text: The procedure gives surgeons access to the structures that blur the jaw-neck transition, so fat can be reduced and the platysma tightened to define the chin-neck angle.

lead: Submental dissection is a surgical technique in which the surgeon reaches the tissues under the chin and upper neck through a small incision in the submental crease. In aesthetic surgery it is used to remove or reposition fat, treat banding of the platysma muscle, and in some cases reach deeper structures that add fullness under the jaw. The aim is a cleaner jawline and a better-defined angle between chin and neck, known as the cervicomental angle.[1]

In looksmaxxing vocabulary it falls in the 'hardmaxx' category of surgical changes. It is rarely offered as a single named procedure; it appears as one step within a neck lift, platysmaplasty or combined face-and-neck operation. Some surgical papers state that a separate submental dissection may be needed to assess pathology and to resect excess platysma laxity that a lateral lift alone does not address.[2]
Surgical literature on submental work is spread across cosmetic neck contouring and unrelated head-and-neck oncologic and reconstructive fields, where submental approaches are also used.

paras: In a neck lift, an incision under the chin allows medial (corset) platysmaplasty, in which the inner edges of the platysma are drawn together at the midline to reduce banding and restore support. Lateral platysmaplasty supports the muscle sideways, and combined approaches address both components. Deep neck work may be added when subplatysmal fat, digastric muscles or submandibular glands contribute to fullness.[1]
Fat removal in the area is meant to be conservative because taking too much can leave a hollow centre and prominent sides, known as 'cobra neck'.[1]

A 2018 paper in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery describing a modified Fogli neck lift reports that the lateral suspension of the platysma to Lore's fascia lifts the anterior neck and defines the cervicomental angle, and that a separate submental dissection may be needed to assess pathology and remove excess platysma laxity.[2]

Two small registered studies explore submental work for double chin: one on a deep-plane intervention in the submental region (12 participants, completed) and one on a fatty flap taken from the double chin for chin enhancement (10 participants, completed).[3][4]

Neck-lift surgery carries risks of bleeding or hematoma, which can compromise skin blood flow, infection, numbness, temporary nerve weakness, contour irregularities and recurrent platysmal bands. Work on the submandibular glands can lead to saliva collection (sialocele) or lower-lip weakness. Temporary nerve weakness usually improves as the nerve recovers.[1]

Evidence consists mainly of surgical technique reports and small registrations. The 2018 modified neck-lift report describes the method,[2] and two small registered studies cover deep-plane submental intervention for double chin and a double-chin fatty flap for chin enhancement.[3][4] No large comparative trial of submental dissection as a stand-alone cosmetic procedure was identified.
